title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook & Benchmarking Suite (Team Wiki)
author: Lena Chen
content:
Overview

This page is the canonical team wiki for the Serving Runtime: architecture decisions, kernel scheduling model, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, known issues, release notes highlight, and operational runbooks. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and performance reviewers. Maintain high-level design decisions here and link to per-component runbooks for incident response.

Goals
- Maintain predictable per-token latency SLOs for hosted and dedicated deployments.
- Provide reproducible profiling and benchmarking methods for model onboarding and performance regressions.
- Describe kernel scheduling heuristics used by the runtime and how to tune them.
- Consolidate runbooks for common performance incidents.

Ownership
- Runtime architecture and kernel scheduling: Runtime team (owner: Marcus Huang)
- Profiling & benchmarks: Performance & Applied-ML (owner: Aisha Patel)
- Release notes & regressions: Runtime release manager (Tomás Rivera)

High-level Architecture

Summary
- The serving runtime is a lightweight orchestrator and execution engine optimized for transformer inference. It consists of three high-level layers: the front-end request router, the scheduling/packing layer, and the execution kernels.

Components
- Request router (service: runtime-router): authenticates, validates, annotates requests with policy (latency/cost/region), and forwards to a scheduling pool.
- Scheduler (service: runtime-scheduler): responsible for batching, device placement, kernel selection, and KV cache coalescing.
- Execution engine (library: rdinfer-kernels): GPU-optimized kernels (attention, matmul, layernorm), memory manager and KV cache manager.
- Telemetry & control plane (service: runtime-telemetry): emits metrics, traces, and accepts runtime config overrides (feature flags, kernel table updates).

Diagram (textual)
- Client -> runtime-router -> runtime-scheduler -> rdinfer-kernels (GPU) -> response
- runtime-telemetry collects metrics at each boundary and exports to Prometheus/Grafana and Honeycomb.

Service-Level Objectives (SLOs)
- 99th percentile per-token latency: hosted API <= 120ms (seq len 128)
- 95th percentile p99 token latency for Dedicated <= 80ms (seq len 128)
- Throughput target per-GPU: 100 tokens/sec for LLaMA-2-13B quantized profile (baseline)
- Error rate SLO: < 0.1% 5xxs per minute

Kernel Scheduling Model

Design Principles
- Prioritize latency-sensitive requests (small seq len, high priority flag) over throughput-oriented batch formation.
- Use continuous batching with per-queue timers to bound tail latency.
- Co-locate KV caches and stateful sessions on the same device to avoid cross-device swaps.

Key Heuristics (current defaults)
- Batch formation: 1ms micro-batch timer + max_batch_size determined by model profile (default 16 for 13B, 8 for 70B).
- Kernel selection: model-architecture + seq_len + quantization_profile -> kernel ABI lookup. Kernels are versioned; fallback policy uses nearest compatible kernel.
- Device placement: affinity rules place pinned sessions to reserved partition; autoscaler updates partition weights when utilization > 70% for 5 minutes.

Tunable Parameters (config table)
- max_batch_size: maximum tokens per batch (per-model)
- microbatch_timer_ms: wait time to collect batch (default 1)
- kv_cache_max_entries_per_session: 1e6 (adjust for long-context models)
- kernel_selection_policy: ["latency_first", "throughput_first", "balanced"]
- device_utilization_high_watermark: 0.70

Example config fragment (runtime-config.yaml)

```yaml
models:
  llama-2-13b:
    max_batch_size: 16
    microbatch_timer_ms: 1
    kernel_selection_policy: latency_first
  mix-70b:
    max_batch_size: 8
    microbatch_timer_ms: 2
    kernel_selection_policy: balanced
scheduling:
  device_utilization_high_watermark: 0.7
  kv_cache_max_entries_per_session: 1000000
```

Profiling Playbook

When to run profiling
- New model onboarding (first production run)
- Significant kernel change (new attention kernel, new quantized path)
- Regression investigation after a release or performance alert

Profiling steps (repeatable checklist)
1. Reproduce the workload: capture representative sample of requests using request-snapshot tool.
2. Run microbenchmarks: per-layer latency with single- and multi-stream configs using rdinfer-benchmark.
3. Full-stack trace: enable TRACE sampling (1%) in runtime-router and collect traces in honeycomb.
4. GPU-level tracing: run with NVTX + CUPTI, capture kernel launch times and memory copies.
5. Analyze KV cache behavior: measure green hits vs misses, swap frequency, and eviction rate.
6. Correlate metrics: align Prometheus metrics (token_latency_seconds, batch_size_histogram, device_utilization) with traces and kernel timelines.

Standard commands
- Capture request snapshot:

```bash
rdctl snapshot capture --service runtime-router --name onboarding-sample-2026-02 --duration 5m --out ./snapshots/onboarding-sample-2026-02.json
```
- Run microbenchmarks:

```bash
rdinfer-benchmark --model llama-2-13b --profile per-layer --batch 1 --seq 128 --out benchmarks/13b-per-layer.json
```
- Collect NVTX trace (remote):

```bash
rdctl tracer start --target worker-42 --type nvtx --duration 60s --out traces/worker-42-nvtx.jfr
```

Benchmarking Suite

Purpose
- Provide reproducible end-to-end benchmarks for throughput, latency, and cost estimates across hardware variants and quantization profiles. Benchmarks feed model catalog performance profiles and the onboarding checklist.

Bench types
- Microbench: per-layer kernel latency and memory usage.
- Latency: P99 token latency measured with realistic request rasters.
- Throughput: max sustained tokens/sec under a variety of concurrency levels.
- Stability: 24-72 hour soak test to detect memory growth or rare-edge faults.

Benchmarking rules
- Run on standardized instance images (AMI: rdinfer-runtime-bench-v3) and pinned CUDA/cuDNN versions listed in release notes.
- Seed PRNG and use fixed prompt sets from prompt-sets-and-benchmarks directory.
- Store benchmark artifacts in /benchmarks/<model>/<date>/ with metadata.json that includes kernel table hash and runtime version.

Sample benchmark invocation

```bash
rdinfer-bench-run --suite latency --model llama-2-13b --seq 128 --concurrency 4 --duration 10m --out /benchmarks/llama-2-13b/2026-02-25/latency.json
```

Release Notes (Runtime highlights)
- 2026-02-20: Kernel v12 rollout: reduced attention kernel global mem copies by 30% for quantized 13B profiles. Default kernel_selection_policy changed to "latency_first" for hosted.
- 2025-12-10: KV cache compaction added to avoid unbounded growth on long-lived sessions; default kv_cache_max_entries_per_session = 1e6.
- 2025-09-01: Initial continuous batching pilot (microbatch_timer_ms = 1) enabled for dedicated clusters.

Known Issues (active)
- ISSUE-1243: Occasional p99 spike (hosted) when autoscaler rebalances partitions. Mitigation: increase device_utilization_high_watermark to 0.75 for the affected pool and rerun soak test. Owner: SRE.
- ISSUE-1301: Rare CUDA launch timeout on NGC 23.x with kernel v11 on 70B model. Workaround: pin kernel v10 or use NGC 22.x. Owner: Runtime team.
- ISSUE-1377: KV cache fragmentation after long-running sessions causing memory pressure. Mitigation: force compaction via admin endpoint /admin/kv/compact and schedule daily compaction for pools with >10k sessions. Owner: Runtime.

Operational Runbooks (high level)

1) p99 latency spike (hosted API)
- Symptoms: sudden increase in token_latency_seconds.p99 across router and scheduler for a specific pool.
- Immediate actions:
  1. Check alerts (PagerDuty) and spike dashboard.
  2. Identify impacted pool and node group: query runtime-telemetry -> pool_utilization and device_utilization.
  3. Temporarily set kernel_selection_policy=throughput_first for the pool to reduce queuing overhead.
  4. If spikes persist, scale up reserved capacity for the pool (apply autoscaler override).
- Postmortem: capture traces + benchmark current kernel table and attach to incident.

2) KV cache OOM on a worker
- Symptoms: OOM events in kernel logs; evictions high; worker restarts.
- Immediate actions:
  1. Drain traffic from worker via runtime-api:mark-drain --node <id>.
  2. Trigger /admin/kv/compact and monitor memory.
  3. If recovered, recycle worker and run soak test.
  4. If not recovered, reprovision worker with larger memory profile.

- Telemetry metrics: PROMETHEUS job="runtime" -> token_latency_seconds, batch_size_histogram, device_utilization, kv_cache_*

Maintenance & Best Practices
- Update kernel table entry and run the full benchmark suite before promoting kernels to hosted production.
- Always attach a microbenchmark artifact and NVTX trace to a kernel change PR.
- Run the stability soak for 48h after significant scheduling changes (timers, max_batch_size, policy).

Appendix: Useful CLI snippets
- List kernel table:

```bash
rdctl kernel list --format json | jq '.[] | {kernel_id, model_compat, version}'
```
- Promote kernel to pool:

```bash
rdctl kernel promote --kernel-id kernel-v12 --pool hosted-eu-west-1
```
